Palestinian, Israeli and international rights groups, and UN findings, have long argued this is not a malfunction of Israeli justice but its design, and that the international system meant to check, and failed to do so, is being taken apart.
For years, Israeli military data has shown conviction rates for Palestinians in Israeli military courts to be anything between 99.74 and 96 percent.

A May 2025 report by Adalah, the legal center for Palestinian citizens of Israel, documents how Israel moved settlement governance in Area C under civilian authority while Palestinians remain under military rule.
Adalah calls the arrangement a system of apartheid and de facto annexation.
Inside Israel, the Knesset keeps adding to the structure.
Adalah’s Discriminatory Laws Database listed over 65 laws that discriminate against Palestinian citizens of Israel or residents of the occupied territory in 2017.

Its November 2025 report reviews more than 30 further laws passed between October 7, 2023 and July 27, 2025, which Adalah says rest on the principle of Jewish ethno-national supremacy that the 2018 Nation-State Law enshrined.
In March 2026, the Knesset passed a death penalty law with 62 votes.
Adalah and four other Israeli rights groups argue its wording excludes Israeli Jewish perpetrators of similar offenses, so that in practice it applies only to Palestinians.
They have petitioned the Supreme Court to annul it.
The Israeli group Yesh Din has tracked police investigations into settler violence against Palestinians since 2005.
Of the files it monitored through 2025, 93.6 percent ended without an indictment, and only about 3 percent ended in a full or partial conviction.
Most closures cited an unidentified suspect or insufficient evidence, which Yesh Din attributes to police failures.
In roughly half of the nearly 30 mass settler attacks it documented between 2023 and late 2025, soldiers or police were present.
Soldiers face similar odds.
In March 2026, the military’s top lawyer dropped charges against five reservists accused of severe sexual and physical abuse against a Palestinian detainee at the Sde Teiman detention camp.
Yesh Din said only two indictments existed over soldiers’ conduct in the Gaza war.
Courts have not interrupted the pattern.
In March 2025, Israel’s Supreme Court unanimously rejected a petition by five Israeli rights groups seeking unimpeded humanitarian aid into Gaza.
The UN Commission of Inquiry concluded in September 2025 that Israel committed genocide in Gaza, joining findings by Amnesty International and B’Tselem.

In October 2026, the commission added that Israel committed crimes against humanity in the West Bank, including extermination, and that military operations since January 2025 caused the largest displacement there since 1967.
In July 2024, the International Court of Justice ruled that Israel’s presence in the occupied territory is unlawful and must end as rapidly as possible.

It also found that Israel’s legislation and measures breach Article 3 of the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination (ICERD), which prohibits racial segregation and apartheid.
In September 2025, UN experts criticized the failure to act on the General Assembly resolution that followed the ruling.
Meanwhile, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defense minister Yoav Gallant in November 2024.
In December 2025, its Appeals Chamber rejected an Israeli challenge and left the warrants in force.

The reaction to the warrants, like that to the UN findings regarding apartheid, genocide and crimes against humanity perpetrated by Israel, has contributed to the failure of international law in delivering justice.

items.title: Madagascar aims to support biodiversity by protecting marine areas

s: In Madagascar, biodiversity goals are being tested by funding challenges and local realities
A booth at COP17 showcases Madagascar’s local communities and biodiversity.
Photo by Sary nalain'ny mpanoratra.
Used with permission.

At the 17th Conference of the Parties (COP17) on biological diversity, held October 19–30, 2026, in Yerevan, Armenia, Madagascar reaffirmed its commitment to protecting its remarkable biodiversity and showcased techniques local community members have implemented.
The country further outlined its plans and priorities for the future and promoted the initiatives it is committed to in order to protect both its terrestrial and marine ecosystems.

This conference was also a strategic opportunity to strengthen green partnerships, develop new collaborations, and to engage with national and international stakeholders involved in biodiversity conservation.

To mark the occasion, Global Voices interviewed Tojotsara Ratefason, Director of the Directorate of Protected Areas, Renewable Natural Resources, and Ecosystems (DAPRNRE), part of the Madagascan government’s Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development (MEDD), at this conference.

The interview focused on Madagascar’s role in implementing the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, the 30×30 global target, conservation funding, and the vital role of local communities, women, and young people in the sustainable protection of Madagascar’s natural heritage.
Raveloaritiana Mamisoa (RM): Where does Madagascar stand on implementing the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework?
Tojotsara Ratefason (TF): Madagascar est confiante dans sa capacité à contribuer à l’atteinte de l’objectif mondial 30×30, aussi bien pour les écosystèmes terrestres que marins.
Notre pays dispose déjà d’un système d’aires protégées qui constitue un socle essentiel pour préserver sa biodiversité exceptionnelle.
Selon les chiffres que nous présentons, ce réseau compte 155 aires protégées terrestres et marines.
Il s’agit d’un acquis important sur lequel nous pouvons nous appuyer pour poursuivre nos efforts de conservation.
Madagascar dispose d’un cadre national de référence pour orienter ses actions en faveur de la biodiversité: la Stratégie et le Plan d’Actions Nationaux pour la Biodiversité (SPANB).
Ce document définit les grandes orientations du pays en matière de conservation, d’utilisation durable et de valorisation de son patrimoine naturel exceptionnel.

Il s’inscrit dans le cadre de la Convention sur la diversité biologique, à laquelle Madagascar est partie, et constitue un instrument essentiel pour traduire les engagements internationaux en actions nationales.
Mais la protection de la biodiversité ne se résume pas au nombre d’aires protégées ni aux superficies concernées.
Notre objectif est avant tout de préserver les écosystèmes, les espèces et les habitats naturels qui font la singularité de Madagascar.
Notre patrimoine naturel est unique au monde et nous avons la responsabilité de le transmettre aux générations futures.
Cette ambition implique également de renforcer la collaboration avec les communautés locales ( vahoaka eny ifotony), qui vivent au contact direct de ces ressources naturelles.
Leur participation est indispensable, car la conservation ne peut pas reposer uniquement sur les décisions du gouvernement.
Elle doit être portée conjointement par les institutions publiques, les gestionnaires des aires protégées et les populations qui vivent dans les territoires concernés.
Nous devons donc trouver les moyens de travailler ensemble, dans une démarche de responsabilité partagée.
Les communautés locales doivent comprendre l’importance de la biodiversité, participer à sa protection et pouvoir constater les bénéfices qu’elles peuvent tirer de sa conservation.

C’est également dans cette perspective que le Ministère de l’Environnement et du Développement Durable cherche à promouvoir les emplois verts et les opportunités économiques liés à la biodiversité unique de Madagascar.

Notre richesse naturelle ne doit pas seulement être considérée comme un patrimoine à protéger: elle peut aussi représenter une source de revenus et de développement pour les populations, à condition d’être valorisée de manière durable.
L’enjeu est de permettre aux communautés de mieux connaître la valeur de leurs ressources naturelles, d’en être fières et de comprendre qu’elles ont tout intérêt à les préserver.

Lorsque les populations constatent que la conservation contribue à améliorer leurs conditions de vie, elles peuvent devenir des partenaires encore plus engagés dans la protection de leur environnement.

items.title: Learning under trees in the era of AI: The paradox of education in Mozambique

s: AI could help bridge educational inequality in a country where thousands of students still learn outdoors

In many communities across Mozambique, formal education still takes place in the open air, under trees, in improvised yards, or inside fragile structures that barely offer protection from the sun and rain.

These so-called outdoor classrooms are not an innovative pedagogical choice, but more often than not, the expression of a structural deficiency: a lack of infrastructure, a shortage of materials, and an estimated deficit of around 12,000 teachers in 2025.
During the rainy season (roughly November to March in Mozambique), the situation becomes more challenging.

In several regions, the school calendar must be adjusted to respond to inclement weather, such as heavy rains that disrupt classes and hinder the continuity of teaching between November and March each year.
In this context, the question arises: What is the place of artificial intelligence (AI) in an educational system that, in many areas of the country, is still fighting for the basics?
In rural districts of provinces like Cabo Delgado, Nampula, and Zambézia, it is common to find classes of students studying under trees.

The Minister of Education, Samaria Tovela, has been evaluating schedule adjustments because, while classes are frequently interrupted during the rainy season, concentration becomes a constant challenge during periods of intense heat.

Without proper blackboards or textbooks, and often with a single teacher responsible for several classes, the learning process becomes irregular and deeply unequal when one million students learn to read and write on the ground.
This scenario highlights a central problem: Learning depends on minimum standards that are not yet guaranteed in Mozambique.
At the same time, one of the biggest obstacles to introducing technologies like AI in rural African contexts is the lack of connectivity.
In Mozambique, about 73 percent of the population lacks internet access, according to 2024 data from the Ministry of Transport and Communications.
Regional inequalities limit these initiatives, despite some progress recorded in recent years.
This limitation directly affects the potential of solutions such as distance learning or digital learning platforms.
Another critical challenge is the linguistic and cultural dimension.
In Africa, where more than 2,000 languages are spoken, only a fraction — around 49 — are represented on digital platforms like Google’s translation service.

Integrating Mozambique’s Indigenous languages, such as Emakhuwa, Xichangana, or Elomwe, into digital educational tools could significantly increase students’ comprehension and engagement, especially in the early years of schooling.
However, implementing these solutions raises practical questions in contexts where access to technology is still limited.

The overwhelming majority of the Mozambican population speaks a Bantu language most frequently at home (81.7 percent), and a portion cannot speak Portuguese at all (41.9 percent), though it is the sole official language of the country due to its colonial history.

Despite this, the media, official government communications, and healthcare institutions continue to privilege Portuguese to the detriment of Bantu languages — the languages of the masses — which, activists argue, constitutes a form of social exclusion.
Emerging initiatives, however, show that it is possible to bridge this gap with the aid of technology.
In Johannesburg, for instance, tech startups are developing AI solutions tailored to African languages.
Offline tools, pre-loaded content, and digital pedagogical assistants are some of the possible solutions to address the deficiencies and limitations of Mozambique’s education system.

While the government does not yet have specific policies to integrate AI tools in schools, advocates say the state could play a central role in integrating technology into the daily lives of students and teachers.

This also involves investing in teacher training; ensuring basic infrastructure; facilitating energy access; and strengthening partnerships with universities, startups, and international organizations.

items.title: Letter from a jailed Azerbaijani political prisoner reveals deadly consequences of silence

s: The Trump administration’s blind eye to severe human rights violations in Azerbaijan is deadly for political prisoners
Bahruz Samadov being brought to Sabail District Court in 2024.
Image by Voice of America, via Wikimedia Commons.
Public domain.
Bahruz Samadov is an Azerbaijani political scientist, peace activist, and PhD candidate at Charles University in Prague, or at least he was until the summer of 2024.
On August 21, 2024, the State Security Service detained Samadov while he was visiting his grandmother in Baku.
Global Voices reported on his arrest at the time, as part of a wider crackdown on critics before Azerbaijan hosted COP29 in November 2024.
Samadov was one of the few Azerbaijani voices to oppose the 2020 Karabakh war.
In his writing for OC Media, Eurasianet and other outlets, he argued for dialogue with Armenia and criticized the expulsion of ethnic Armenians from Karabakh.
Prosecutors charged him with high treason based on his WhatsApp exchanges with Armenian peace activists and on publicly available information.
Samadov denied the charges and called himself a “prisoner of peace.
His lawyer argued that the prosecution’s theory of “ indirect espionage ” was vague and had no basis in case law.
On June 23, 2025, after a closed-door trial, the Baku Grave Crimes Court sentenced him to 15 years in prison.
The Baku Court of Appeal upheld the verdict in September 2025, and the Supreme Court did the same in September 2026.

Amnesty International, which considers him arbitrarily imprisoned, reports that he has been held in solitary confinement and denied medical care, and that he has twice attempted suicide, most recently in his Supreme Court hearing.
Below, Global Voices publishes a letter Samadov wrote from prison and asked us to share.

The 2024 summer holidays ended in a nightmare: while visiting Baku, my home city, from my doctoral studies in Prague, I was detained by the notorious State Security Service of Azerbaijan and soon was charged with “high treason.”

Studying the ideological tenets of the hegemonic regime in my homeland, I directly connected its durability to the conflict between Azerbaijan and Armenia, revealing the narratives of “national unity” under the “savior strongman.”
During and after the outbreak of the 2020 War in Karabakh, I criticized the deployment of military means.
Between 2021–2024, I partook in various conferences and meetings across Europe, presenting my perspective and calling for a meaningful and inclusive policy of peace and co-existence.
The Azerbaijani regime, having years of the crackdown experience, is aggressively intolerant to any kinds of contestation, and especially targets the independent academic voices.
When the repressive machinery was re-launched in late 2023, the regime started the total crackdown on civil society, independent media, politicians, and academicians.
In private communications, more than five political prisoners connected it to the worsened relations with the Biden administration.
The latter was highly critical to the human rights violations in Azerbaijan.
Weeks before leaving the White House, Blinken invited human rights defender Rufat Safarov to Washington to receive the Human Rights Defender Award.
Several hours after visiting the US Embassy in Baku, Safarov was arrested and accused of hooliganism and fraud.
It was an open signal to the US that the leaving administration had no power to endorse the Azerbaijani critical voices.
The Azerbaijani government acted differently with the Trump administration.
The August 8, 2025 meeting and the peace agreement was the soon-disappeared sign of hope for us.

Even if the peace agreement did not include any references to human rights, the current administration’s plans for the long-term involvement in the region brought hopes for at least minimal reforms in Azerbaijan.

items.title: While Russia tries to manipulate information, local civil society is teaching Armenians media literacy

s: A group of journalists and activists created ‘Verify This,’ a platform where users can find reliable information

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South.
It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.
Armenia is a small, landlocked country that has, for years, relied on Russian support in its long-term conflict with the neighboring oil-rich and authoritarian country, Azerbaijan.
However, Armenia received a blow from Russia in 2022–2023, when it was not supported by Russian military forces during its conflict over the Nagorno-Karabakh region.

In September 2023, Azerbaijan launched a large-scale military offensive, expelled the entire Armenian population from Nagorno-Karabakh, dissolved the government of the region, and incorporated the territory into Azerbaijan.

After this incident, when Russia did not support Armenia with its peacekeeping troops, likely because Vladimir Putin was already engaged in a full-scale invasion and war with Ukraine, Armenia visibly changed its attitude toward Russia.
Armenian Prime Minister ​Nikol Pashinyan started to work in earnest towards the goal of European Union ⁠membership for his South Caucasus country and increased diplomatic communication with the US.
He was re-elected on June 7, 2026.
The election took place amid reports of Russian interference.

Reuters, citing anonymous Western intelligence officials and documents, reported covert Russian efforts to undermine Pashinyan and support pro-Russian candidates, including through disinformation campaigns.
These elections showed how information warfare has expanded beyond social media.
It now included fake news websites, AI-generated videos and material presented as reporting by reputable international media outlets.
According to the US-based disinformation monitoring organization NewsGuard, a Russia-linked campaign circulated 31 fabricated stories about Pashinyan in just one week.
The stories accused him of election fraud and of trying to drag Armenia into a war with Russia.
Some of this material imitated international media outlets such as France 24 and Politico.
Other stories impersonated Armenian news outlets, including Armenpress and CivilNet.
With the proliferation of generative AI, disinformation and propaganda campaigns have become increasingly sophisticated.
Armenia’s experience shows how these campaigns operate in a country moving away from its longstanding reliance on Russia.
At the same time, Armenian journalists and civil society are working hard to build media literacy to counter disinformation campaigns.
This Digital Spark Spotlight interview is about one of these projects — “ Verify First,” a platform where users can find reliable information.

Global Voices interviewed Armin Asryan, a member of the group of journalists, editors, and activists behind the media literacy project “Verify First,” which tackles Russian information manipulation and propaganda.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Spark project.
Armin Asryan (AA): We are a group of enthusiasts, operating through the ‘Socio Club’ — Social and Information NGO — and dedicated to driving positive change in Armenia’s information landscape.
We chose to get involved with the Digital Spark project because we were thrilled to see an opportunity to actively contribute to a healthier, more reliable information space on social networks.

In response to the growing challenges of online misinformation, we developed a targeted initiative to produce six educational video reels focused on practical fact-checking techniques and media literacy, designed to equip everyday social media users with the tools to spot and counter misleading content.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?
AA: The Armenian social media space is heavily impacted by disinformation, low-quality content, and online hostility.
Every day, social media feeds reveal content that not only disappoints users but also generates widespread panic and fear.

items.title: How medical neglect killed Alfredo Díaz in a Venezuelan cell

s: The state deprived a former governor of medical care despite clear warning signs
Illustration made with AI by Runrunes.
Used with permission.
Read our special coverage on Venezuela’s fight for democracy and the political crisis that has unfolded since the 2024 presidential elections, after the documented allegations of electoral fraud.

This is the first installment of a series by Luis Carlos Díaz covering cases of torture, neglect, and cruel treatment against political prisoners, based on the latest report by the UN Fact-Finding Mission.
Originally published in Runrunes and translated by Caracas Chronicles.
To kick off this series, it is worth examining how the latest report by the UN Fact-Finding Mission (FFM) on Venezuela was constructed.

Based on 213 confidential interviews with 121 victims, relatives, and witnesses, as well as forensic data and judicial documents, the report matches the rigorous evidentiary threshold of “reasonable grounds to believe.”
Despite the Venezuelan state’s complete refusal to cooperate, the FFM’s technical findings expose a crucial reality.

Following the United States’ military intervention on January 3 and the capture of Nicolás Maduro, interim president Delcy Rodríguez announced cabinet reshuffles, released hundreds of prisoners, and oversaw a decline in long-term detentions.

However, the United Nations (UN) found that at least 18 high-ranking officials previously implicated in human rights violations and crimes against humanity remain in key positions of power or military command, including Diosdado Cabello, Gustavo González López, Alexander Granko Arteaga, and Vladimir Padrino López.
The core architecture of state repression remains fully intact, providing the structural context for the individual cases documented in this series.
Before delving into the case of Alfredo Díaz, I want to address a question that often lingers when we discuss the UN reports: What is all this work actually for?
What happens to a report like this once it is published?
The Independent International Fact-Finding Mission was not created on a whim, nor was it meant to issue a general diagnosis and stop there.

It was established by the Human Rights Council under Resolution 42/25 in 2019, with a specific mandate: to document the most serious crimes committed in the country to combat impunity, ensure accountability for those responsible, and secure justice for victims.
This carries practical consequences, even if they are not immediate.
The FFM is an investigative body, one of only seven active mechanisms of its kind worldwide.
That alone underscores how extraordinary our situation is, and how resilient civil society has been in organizing to secure its renewal on four separate occasions.
In October, countries in the Human Rights Council voted to extend its mandate for two additional years.

Whenever the FFM concludes there are “reasonable grounds to believe” that an individual participated in a human rights violation, that finding is preserved in secure databases with case files, testimonies, and evidence.
This material is not lost, even if no Venezuelan court is willing to use it.
This documentation has already had real effects outside Venezuela.
The report notes, for instance, that a federal court in Argentina issued an extradition request in June 2026 against a Spain-based former Venezuelan military officer linked to the 2014 repression.

The court relied on the principle of universal jurisdiction — the legal framework allowing a country to prosecute grave international crimes committed elsewhere, when justice is denied in the country of origin.
That officer was named in the 2025 special report on the Bolivarian National Guard.

items.title: Ecuadorian youth unite against neoliberal models and state violence

s: In Quito, in defiance of the Jóvenes en Acción (Youth in Action) strategy with which Daniel Noboa’s government has attempted to boost employment for young people, thousands of students have been staging marches and sit-ins in streets and squares, demanding medicines, security, and a budget for education.
Their protests show a clear departure from the traditional approach to collective mobilization in Ecuador.

Previously, these types of events have been led by the Confederation of Indigenous Nationalities of Ecuador (CONAIE); trade union groups such as the Ecuador Confederation of Free Trade Union Organizations (CEOSL), the United Workers’ Front (FUT), and the National Union of Educators (UNE); as well as feminist, anti-mining, and environmentalist movements.

However, on the afternoon of Saturday, October 10, 2026, the Ecuadorian capital witnessed a massive mobilization led by high school and university students, who gathered outside the Central University to march to Quito’s Historic Center.
The call was made by the Autonomous Resistance Front (FARO), which comprises several youth collectives:
Quienes encabezaban la marcha anunciaron su finalización y llamaron a dispersarse.
Sin embargo, la multitud continúa avanzando por las calles de Quito, desafiando el asedio policial y haciendo resonar consignas contra el Gobierno de Daniel Noboa. @teleSURtv
What is happening in Quito is striking: Those leading the march announced its conclusion and called for the crowd to disperse.
Nevertheless, the throng continues to move through the streets of Quito, defying a police blockade and chanting slogans against the government of Daniel Noboa.

With their presence in the streets, the young people of Quito denounced the deterioration of public services, including the lack of medical supplies and medicines in hospitals, cuts to the public education budget, low youth employment, a persistent increase in insecurity, and forced disappearances at the hands of state agents.
Their slogans also spoke out against the genocide in Palestine and the United States’ interventionism in Latin America.
According to figures from the National Institute of Statistics and Census (INEC), 40 percent of unemployed people in Ecuador are between 15 and 24 years old.
Labor precariousness, a dearth of opportunities, and the high cost of living are just some of the factors affecting the country’s youth.

Meanwhile, on October 30, the Noboa administration launched its third edition of “Youth in Action,” an initiative aimed at the 18-29 demographic, who are promised temporary, two-month jobs with a salary of USD 400 per month.

The measure has faced harsh criticism from various academics and civic sector representatives, who maintain that the absence of a comprehensive, long-term vision proves its inefficiency in tackling youth unemployment.

In November 2025, Ecuador’s National Assembly approved the country’s 2026 budget proposal, which hit public universities, polytechnic schools, co-financed institutions, and postgraduate programs with an allocated budget reduction of approximately USD 99 million.

The decrease was reflected in the absence of student scholarships, non-existent investment in research, and a reduction in available slots to access free public higher education, which is established as a fundamental right in Article 26 of Ecuador’s Constitution.

During the peaceful youth march, participants chanted slogans like “Out Noboa, out,” “If the people have no peace, the government won’t either,” and “Noboa, fascist,” expressing indignation against a government they believe has failed to solve social problems that affect not only young people, but the majority of the population.
Direct rejection of deficient public administration, coupled with excessive state violence against citizens, motivated the students to protest.
Many videos posted on social media captured police aggression against peaceful demonstrators, as well as physical assaults on journalists as they reported on the protests.
teleSUR reporter Elena Rodríguez Yánez shared her experience on X:

items.title: Trinbagonian Jason Jones wins landmark Privy Council judgement deeming ‘buggery laws’ unconstitutional

s: Trinbagonian LGBTQ+ activist Jason Jones at the Hall of Justice in Port of Spain, Trinidad, after the landmark 2018 judgement that deemed Trinidad and Tobago’s ‘buggery laws’ unconstitutional.
Photo by Maria Nunes, used with permission.

Eight years and nearly seven months after Justice Devindra Rampersad ruled, in the case of LGBTQ+ activist Jason Jones vs. the Attorney General of Trinidad and Tobago, that Sections 13 and 16 of Trinidad and Tobago’s Sexual Offences Act Chapter 11:28 — which criminalise anal sex between consenting adults — were “unconstitutional,” the United Kingdom’s Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, still Trinidad and Tobago’s highest appellate court, overturned a 2025 Court of Appeal decision to keep the country’s “buggery law” on the books.
It has been a long road to get to this point.

Almost as soon as the 2018 judgement went in Jones’ favour, the Trinidad and Tobago government announced its intention to appeal, with then Attorney General Faris Al-Rawi stating, “The rights of equality in the Constitution are clearly expressed.
A first-instance decision is not the only decision to rely upon to settle the law. [An appeal] is only prudent so we can conclusively put the matter to rest.”
Almost seven years later, on March 25, 2025, a local appeal court overturned the 2018 judgement.
Jones was disappointed but not deterred, vowing to take the case all the way to the Privy Council.
He remained true to his word and on November 10, 2026 — quite ironically, given that it was a colonial-era law — British lawlords finally ruled on the matter.

There were a few key issues to be considered, including how to address the controversial “savings law” clause in the legislation — laws enacted prior to colonised countries becoming independent and developing their own constitutions, that were “saved” to remain in force even afterwards.

Jones maintained that the clause had “no place in a 21st century democracy” and that Trinidad and Tobago’s government and parliament were “derelict” in not removing it, especially after the twin-island nation became a republic in 1976.

The Council’s conclusion in the case, which deemed that “Sections 13 and 16 of the SOA 1986 have been shown by Mr Jones ‘not to be reasonably justifiable in a society that has a proper respect for the rights and freedoms of the individual,’” caused it to agree with the 2018 ruling and deny the attorney-general’s cross-appeal.
With other regional territories also using the Privy Council as their highest court of appeal, the result could augur well for similar actions across the wider Caribbean.

As Jones told reporters on the steps of Trinidad’s Hall of Justice following his 2018 triumph, “The human rights issue is not just local […] Over 75 million Commonwealth citizens are criminalised using similar laws — 37 Commonwealth nations — criminalised similarly to Trinidad.”

Still, Jones — who launched his legal challenge in 2015 — says that the fight continues: “Whilst I welcome this judgement, it does not, however, address the main issues of human rights and equality for LGBTQ+ people which have been denied using British colonial-era laws across the Commonwealth and beyond.
It is a stance echoed by many LGBTQ+ organisations, as issues of discrimination, language, and societal and religious acceptance also persist.
Jones is well aware that changing these attitudes requires broader reform and re-education.
The law lords’ unanimous, provisional view, however, was that the original High Court remedy should stand.
However, there may well be written submissions still to come.

items.title: Can regenerative school gardens strengthen food security in Cameroon?

s: The school gardens are helping alleviate food insecurity while providing learning opportunities and empower community members
Students of Blessed Bilingual Education Centre preparing the farm.
Photo by Support Humanity Cameroon.
Used with permission.
Students of Blessed Bilingual Education Centre in Ebang, Cameroon’s Centre Region, have recorded their first harvest of the 2026–2027 school year.

Through the Climate Change and Innovation Club, an initiative introduced in 2024 by Support Humanity Cameroon (SUHUCAM) to connect environmental education with practical action, students planted huckleberry in their school garden at the start of the academic year in September.

Like them, pupils in Cameroon’s North West Region are managing school gardens and growing food using regenerative practices such as minimal tillage, composting, organic manure and fruit-tree grafting.
Cameroon continues to face a decade-long humanitarian crisis, contributing to food insecurity in the Anglophone regions and Far North, while displacing thousands of families.
Earlier this year, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies reported worsening hunger among nearly 6,000 Cameroonian households following an assessment.
More than 3.3 million people were struggling to find enough food, while about 64 percent of households experienced severe food insecurity.
Children are among those affected.
Nationwide, 29 percent of children under five experience chronic malnutrition.
Beyond its nutritional consequences, food insecurity can also affect children’s ability to learn and participate in school activities.
According to the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), hunger can impair concentration and memory and affect classroom attendance.
In February 2026, the organisation reported that only 2.8 percent of primary school pupils in Cameroon received a free hot meal at school, highlighting the limited reach of school lunch programmes.
Conflict, climate-related disasters, agricultural losses and rising staple food prices are among the main drivers of this crisis.
To combat persistent food insecurity, educators and nonprofit organisations are partnering to teach children how to grow their own food.
In Bamenda, North West region of Cameroon, the Youth Association for Climate Action (YACA) runs the ADAPT Programme, which engages 70 pupils from two nursery and primary schools.

Created after a survey revealed that few schools had gardens or provided environmental education, the ADAPT Club has established gardens with five sections: nurseries, vegetables, fruit trees, composting and tubers.
Muluh Kelly Vughose, Programme coordinator for ADAPT, says pupils are involved in more than just planting.
“Our volunteers, together with the teachers and pupils, designed each garden.
Children are also involved in learning basic agricultural skills like plantain propagation and grafting of fruit trees.
The club holds two sessions each week, lasting about two hours.

In the same region, in Nkambe and neighbouring villages, pupils from six primary and two secondary schools are learning agricultural skills through the Smart School Gardens Project, launched by Youth Development Organisation – Yodo Cameroon.
Schools have received wheelbarrows, watering cans and compost manure to support the project.
“During the two years of implementation, I have watched these pupils and students care for plants from seed germination until harvest,” says Ekoaba Cevie, Yodo Cameroon’s Programme Coordinator.
The gardens produce cabbage, huckleberry, carrots and Irish potatoes.

Meanwhile, SUHUCAM’s regenerative school garden programme in the Centre region combines fruit trees, including guava, soursop, orange and papaya, with plantains and produce such as huckleberry, cabbage and waterleaf.
Through these activities, pupils are learning techniques such as composting, plant propagation and grafting.
Children are embracing the school gardens with enthusiasm, discovering the importance of food production and sustainability through practical experience.
Queeninver Ngwangung, SUHUCAM’s Youth and Advocacy Lead, explains:
“Rather than simply teaching students about sustainable agriculture, food security or climate action, we give them opportunities to practice these concepts,” she said.

“Through growing food, managing organic waste and caring for their gardens, we have observed that students have learnt that environmental solutions can begin with everyday actions within their own schools.”

items.title: Justice is the infrastructure the world keeps forgetting

s: The world cannot build prosperous economies, peaceful societies or resilient democracies while neglecting its people’s everyday justice needs.
This post by Jude Udo Ilo is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “ Justice as infrastructure.
In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law ( HiiL ) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society.
You can support this coverage by donating here.
Imagine visiting a hospital with a serious illness, only to discover that every patient receives the same medication, regardless of their symptoms.
We would rightly call this a failure of healthcare.
Yet this is remarkably close to how justice is delivered in much of the world.
We have built justice systems around institutions rather than people, procedures rather than problems, and legal traditions rather than lived realities.

We measure progress by the number of courts constructed, judges appointed and laws enacted, while paying insufficient attention to whether ordinary people can actually resolve the disputes disrupting their lives.
This institutional obsession reflects a deeper failure in how we understand development.
Justice is not simply a legal service or a moral aspiration.
It is essential for economic and social infrastructure.
Our collective failure to treat it as such is undermining development, deepening inequality and threatening global stability.

With the level of discontent across the world, distrust in institutions, poverty and inequality, and growing footprints of violent conflict, we need to refocus on what is necessary to heal our bleeding world.
When governments and international financial institutions discuss infrastructure, the conversation invariably turns to roads, bridges, electricity and digital connectivity.
These investments matter.
But what happens when a highway project becomes trapped in unresolved land disputes; when a small business cannot recover payments from a supplier?
When a woman cannot claim her inheritance, or communities cannot secure remedies for environmental destruction?
Physical infrastructure cannot deliver its promised benefits when the institutions and mechanisms for resolving grievances are inaccessible, ineffective or distrusted.
Justice is the soft infrastructure that allows economies and societies to function.
For businesses, it provides the certainty necessary for investment, contract enforcement and growth.
For individuals, it protects rights, livelihoods and opportunities.
For communities, it creates peaceful pathways for addressing grievances before they escalate into confrontation.
Without functioning justice systems, economic development becomes fragile and social stability increasingly precarious.

The World Justice Project estimates that the economic costs of legal problems, including lost income, health impacts and expenses of seeking resolution, average 1.7 percent of GDP across the countries studied.
The scale of the problem is staggering.
The Justice for All report estimates that 5.2 billion people lack meaningful access to justice.
HiiL's research demonstrates that everyday legal problems are widespread, while effective, satisfactory resolutions remain elusive.
This is a crisis of development.
Across the world, unresolved grievances are quietly eroding the foundations of social cohesion.
In parts of Africa, disputes over land ownership, natural resources and community rights have contributed to recurring tensions.
In fragile and conflict-affected societies, the absence of credible mechanisms for resolving grievances can deepen mistrust and reinforce cycles of violence.
But justice failures are hardly confined to developing countries.
From housing disputes and discriminatory employment practices to unequal access to legal representation, even wealthy democracies struggle to ensure that justice works for everyone.
The consequences extend beyond those directly affected.
When people repeatedly encounter institutions that cannot protect their rights or resolve their problems, confidence in public authority deteriorates.
When people encounter injustice, they can easily become the enemy of the state.
And where legitimate institutions fail, alternative systems of enforcement emerge.
Sometimes these are constructive community mechanisms.
At other times, they involve coercion, exploitation or violence.
We cannot sustainably address insecurity while ignoring the injustices that help fuel it.

items.title: Homeland Security says Minneapolis woman shot by ICE officer dies

s: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) reported Wednesday that a woman shot by a U.S.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer in Minneapolis has died.
Homeland Security officials have described the shooting as an act of self-defense, while Minnesota governor Tim Walz and Minneapolis mayor Jacob Frey have pushed back on this account.

DHS spokesperson Tricia McLaughlin stated that the shooting occurred when ICE officers fired "defensive shots" in response to the woman "attempting to run over our law enforcement officers" with her vehicle.
Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem said the woman’s conduct was "an act of domestic terrorism."
The incident was under active investigation, with the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension (BCA) and the FBI taking over the case.
Walz said the state was working to learn more and asked residents to remain calm, while protest activity continued at the scene and a substantial law-enforcement presence remained in the area.
According to ABC News, Jacob Frey, the mayor of Minneapolis, said in a statement that he was aware of the shooting and urged the agency to depart the city at once.
On social media, he stated the involvement of federal immigration officers was "causing chaos in our city.
He added that the city is "demanding ICE to leave the city immediately," and said officials "stand rock solid with our immigrant and refugee communities.
In a news conference, he disputed the account that the woman's vehicle was weaponized against the agent.

items.title: Roblox player uncovers cheating, awarded Guinness World Record

s: In early January, international media reported that Quinten Delaere, an 18-year-old, had been officially recognized by Guinness World Records after exposing cheating on the Roblox platform.
Delaere, known online as 'kannotlogin', used data analysis to demonstrate that the top times on the global leaderboard were achieved using illegal scripts.
Delaere was competing in a speed-running event for the game Ultimate Easy Obby.
The event was an official collaboration between Roblox and Guinness World Records.
Players had to complete a digital obstacle course as fast as possible.
According to JV, after weeks of practice, Delaere posted a time of 5 minutes and 48.96 seconds.
Before the competition closed, three unknown accounts posted times around 5 minutes and 42 seconds.
JV reported that Delaere, posting on Reddit, believed the times were humanly impossible.
Delaere conducted a digital forensic analysis and compiled a report alleging that the new records were fraudulent.
The report cited three technical points.
First, the analysis pointed to the timestamps of the badges earned by the rival accounts.
The data showed that badges were unlocked in a non-chronological order.
Delaere’s report described the non-chronological order as consistent with the use of teleportation scripts in a normally linear course.
Second, the top accounts were missing specific digital items in their inventory.
Players who cross the finish line automatically receive a 'digital receipt' (an in-game item).
The suspect accounts lacked this item.
According to Kotaku, Delaere argued that "this proved he never actually touched the finish line trigger; he likely teleported a coordinate script to the end-game lobby."
PCGamesN reported that Delaere’s investigation found expired items in the players’ inventories.
Delaere also submitted a frame-by-frame video analysis of his own run to calculate the theoretical maximum speed, arguing that the rival times were mathematically unachievable.
"I took my best run and calculated the theoretical maximum time save possible (perfect pixels, zero drag).
Even with a TAS (Tool-Assisted Speedrun) level of perfection, the times the cheaters posted were mathematically impossible within the game’s physics engine."
Delaere submitted his findings to the Guinness World Records headquarters in London.
MeriStation reported that, after an internal review, the organization concluded Delaere was correct, disqualified the other accounts, and awarded him the official world record.
The challenged times were removed from the database.
The time set by Delaere was officially recognized as the new world record.

items.title: Grateful Dead rhythm guitarist Bob Weir dies, aged 78

s: On Saturday, the family of American musician and songwriter Bob Weir announced that he had died surrounded by loved ones.
The former guitarist and vocalist of the rock band Grateful Dead was 78.
His family announced his death via Instagram, noting that he had recently fought a cancer diagnosis but died due to "underlying lung issues".
The announcement did not specify the date of Weir's death.

Weir played rhythm guitar and sang with American psychedelic rock band the Grateful Dead for decades, and also wrote some of their songs, including the hit "Sugar Magnolia", a staple of Grateful Dead concerts.
He also had a long solo career, making various groups with fellow Grateful Dead alumni, and playing live until months before his death.

Weir was born Robert Hall Parber on October 16, 1947, in San Francisco, California, and grew up in the San Francisco Bay Area, spending some time going to school in Colorado, where he met future Grateful Dead member John Perry Barlow.
Weir started playing guitar at age 13 and gravitated to a local bluegrass scene, where he first encountered Jerry Garcia playing banjo.
On December 31, 1965, Garcia and Weir agreed to form their own group called Mother McCree's Uptown Jug Champions, which evolved into the Grateful Dead.
Weir played rhythm guitar, and sang for the group, for decades.

He also explored a solo career and variety of other groups outside of the Grateful Dead starting in the 1970s, including Kingfish, Bobby and the Midnites, RatDog, Furthur, The Other Ones, The Dead, Wolf Bros, and Dead & Company.
All groups featured fellow Grateful Dead collaborators and explored genres from country rock to jam band to jazz-influenced roots rock with a basis in blues and country.

His vocal contributions were mostly only harmonies and as a backup singer, but he took lead on several tracks, including Grateful Dead anthem "Truckin'", a song noted by the Library of Congress as a national treasure in 1997.

Outside of musical performance, Weir has also established Tamalpais Research Institute, a virtual performance platform, and was active in politics, advocating for several causes, including environmentalism, poverty relief, and issues related to the arts.
He had stayed active in the Bay Area music scene, performing live with local musicians and co-owning the venue Sweetwater Music Hall in Mill Valley, California.
He is survived by wife Natascha and daughters Chloe and Monet, as well as other family.

items.title: Boy retrieves Nintendo Switch locked away in gun safe, and shoots his father

s: On January 13, the night of his 11th birthday, a boy allegedly shot his father with a gun retrieved from a gun safe in the family's home in Duncannon Borough, Pennsylvania.
According to court documents, the boy told investigators he became mad after his father told him to go to bed.
Police charged the boy with criminal homicide.
The court has refused bail.
The boy was placed in Perry County Prison, and an initial court hearing was scheduled for January 22, according to a criminal docket.
According to court documents, the mother was asleep until the gunshot woke her.
When state police arrived at the home, the boy was heard shouting "Daddy's dead" and was overheard telling his mother, "I killed Daddy."
Police arrived on scene around 3:20 a.m.
Eastern Standard Time (08:20 UTC).
According to the affidavit, the boy told the police that he did not think about what would happen after the shot, saying he was "mad and did not think about that."

According to court documents, the boy told investigators he found a key to the gun safe in a drawer and unlocked the safe in an attempt to get back his Nintendo Switch, then loaded the gun and shot his father.
The Nintendo Switch had been placed in a gun safe located in the parents' bedroom.
The parents adopted the boy in 2018, according to a report by the New York Post.

items.title: Bruce Gallanter interviews Elliott Sharp, Joe Fonda at Downtown Music Gallery event

s: On January 12, Downtown Music Gallery in New York City hosted a public reading and discussion featuring Elliott Sharp and Joe Fonda, followed by their first-ever live performance together as a duo.
The event also included extended, in-person interviews conducted by Bruce Gallanter focused on the artists’ recently published books.
Sharp read first from his new book, Feedback: Translations from the IrRational, and was then interviewed by Gallanter.
Fonda then discussed passages from his new book, My Life in the World of Music.
After these talks, Sharp and Fonda, who have known each other since 1978, performed together using a variety of extended techniques.
Sharp played his electroacoustic guitar through an amplifier, while Fonda played acoustic contrabass with no amplification.
Note: This interview has been edited for clarity.
((Bruce Gallanter)) : Elliott, I have a few questions for you.
((Elliott Sharp)) : Okay, if we have time.
((Gallanter)) Yeah.
When did you pick up the guitar?
((Gallanter)) And you would listen to mostly rock music at that point?
((Sharp)) Yeah, and classical music.
I played classical piano as a kid and classical clarinet after that when I was eight, when the piano gave me asthma (in my interpretation) that nearly killed me.
So I played clarinet, then I got an electric guitar, and that was it.
The clarinet went by the wayside.

Also, I got kicked out of wind ensemble and marching band because I came back from a summer residency after my junior year with long hair and a beard, and Al Renino, the band director, would have none of that.
((Gallanter)) When you first started playing, were you playing kind of blues rock stuff at the beginning?

((Sharp)) Well, making psychedelic noise, I was very inspired by readings I was doing in Cage, I was an electronics geek, so I was building my own circuits and experimenting with tape delays and building ring modulators and fuzz, so I was making a lot of noise... and trying to learn Jeff Beck's guitar playing from the Yardbirds records and then Jimi Hendrix.
I mean, Jeff Beck's playing, at least I could find the notes.
With Hendrix, it was beyond me at first, it was just so sonic, you know, but yeah, and a lot of blues, country blues, playing a lot of slide.
((Gallanter)) So you played in blues rock bands?
((Sharp)) Yeah.
I was playing, the first blues band I was in was called the MFBB, the MotherFucking Blues Band, and I was playing bass in that.
((Sharp)) That was '68, '69 when I was still in high school.
I started playing guitar and pedal steel in bands in Ithaca in 1970 when I was at Cornell.
((Gallanter)) OK.
That's where you went to school first?

((Gallanter)) So you've had I mean, I know that most people think of you more as avant-garde kind of noisemaker, even with the guitar and the other instruments that you play, but it seems that you've always had that blues thing.
((Sharp)) Yeah, blues.
And I went for a long period of playing bebop and studying with Roswell Rudd.
But I'll still do gigs occasionally, playing like for a party, playing some blues or jazz or funk tunes, and people come and say, well, I didn't know you actually knew how to play guitar.
((Gallanter)) Somebody said the same thing today when we had on that Terraplane CD.
They said, this is Elliott Sharp?
He plays the blues?
I said, he plays the blues really well, and he's obviously studied it, because you've been doing records of that, starting with that Hoosegow record.

items.title: White House deletes Truth Social post portraying Obamas as apes

s: The White House has deleted a post on Donald Trump's social media account containing a video portraying former United States President Barack Obama and his wife Michelle Obama as apes.
The video triggered a backlash from American politicians, including from Trump's own Republican Party.
After initially defending the post, the White House removed the post from Trump's account in response to backlash, according to the BBC.
A White House official stated that a staff member had mistakenly posted the video.
Trump himself has stated that he did not see the full video prior to it being posted and according to ABC News Australia, he refused to apologize, stating "I didn't make a mistake.
I mean, I give - I look at a lot - thousands of things."
Senator Tim Scott, who is both African American and a Republican, referred to the video as "the most racist thing I've ever seen out of this White House."
The video, which lasts 62 seconds, used the song The Lion Sleeps Tonight as background music and references allegations of electoral fraud in the 2020 United States presidential election.

In addition to the Obamas, it portrays various other Democratic Party politicians as animals, such as United States Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Zohran Mamdani, the mayor of New York City, and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton.
Former United States President Joe Biden, like the Obamas, is portrayed as an ape eating a banana.
According to the BBC, the video is believed to have originated from conservative meme creator Xerias, who shared the post on X in October 2025.

items.title: Göbeklitepe, Taş Tepeler and life 12,000 years ago exhibition opens in Berlin, Germany

s: On February 6, 2026, the "Gebaute Gemeinschaft - Göbeklitepe, Taş Tepeler and Life 12,000 Years Ago" exhibition opened at Berlin's James-Simon-Galerie.
Scheduled to be running until July 19, 2026, the show featured 93 archaeological artifacts brought from Turkey from Göbeklitepe and the Taş Tepeler region.
Stone sculptures from the UNESCO World Heritage site Göbeklitepe were exhibited alongside finds from Karahantepe, Sayburç, and Çakmaktepe.
Everyday objects and jewelry were on display.

Spanish photographer Isabel Muñoz's contemporary interpretations framing the hunter-gatherers' transition to settled life across eight thematic sections, which were exhibited in Spain earlier in 2024, were also included in the exhibition.
The exhibition was curated by Barbara Helwing (Vorderasiatisches Museum) and Necmi Karul (Istanbul University) in collaboration with Şanlıurfa Archaeology Museum and the Taş Tepeler research project.
It was the first time some exhibits were brought abroad, after having been exhibited in several locations in Turkey.

items.title: Caloundra through to next round of 2026 Australia Cup preliminaries

s: Caloundra have qualified for the next round of soccer's Australia Cup qualifiers with a 4-1 win over Pacific Pines on Saturday night in Meridan Plains, Queensland.
"[We had a] good second half," said Caloundra captain Kaine Frew.
"Obviously first competitive match [of the year] tonight.
It was good for the boys to get the cobwebs out.
We've played a few easier sort of preseason games and obviously they've come up from the Gold Coast."
Three goals in the space of ten minutes secured Caloundra's advancement after the scores were tied at 1 all at half time.
"We started a bit slow and obviously we got a few new players," Frew said.
"So we're all just still gelling.
But yeah, no, it was a really good second half.
We're happy with that.
And we'll take that into training next week and be ready for round one."
Caloundra's next game is scheduled to be against Brisbane Knights as part of the Football Queensland Premier League 2 opening round on February 28.
"[Brisbane Kights are] a big club, but we really don't know [what to expect], to be honest," said Frew.
"We're just going to worry about ourselves.
Obviously, we think we can be competitive this year there's no doubt about that.
As long as we can play 90 minutes.
Not like tonight where, you know, first half an hour wasn't great.
We need to play like we did in the second half for the whole game."

items.title: Musical performance presented by Striped Light in Long Island City, New York showcases four performers

s: On the evening of February 16, 2026, an audience gathered at an undisclosed location to see a performance by three experimental musical acts in Long Island City, Queens, New York, as part of the ongoing Striped Light series of events.
A volunteer contributor to Wikinews attended the event as a reporter.
There were somewhere between forty and a hundred people in attendance.
The doors opened for the event at 7:30 p.m.
New York time (0030 UTC).
Jennifer Gersten played the first set, as a soloist.
She played the violin using a variety of techniques, holding it in a traditional manner as well as on her lap at times.
Jack Langdon played the second set, also as a soloist.
He played a Native American flute through amplification, taking advantage of the opportunity to explore extended techniques and unusual sounds with the flute.
John King and Leyya Mona Tawil performed the third set as a duo.

King played guitar while using electronics and a laptop positioned on a table in front of him, while Tawil worked with electronics, multiple microphones, and unconventional objects; at one point, she danced on the amplified stage.
In contrast to the earlier sets, this was a high-volume set.
Striped Light is an ongoing series curated by David Watson and Ian Douglas-Moore.
The location of the performances is only revealed to performers and people who purchase tickets.

items.title: Green Party wins major by-election in northern England city of Manchester

s: The Green Party of England and Wales candidate Hannah Spencer has been declared the winner of Thursday's by-election in Gorton and Denton, a parliamentary constituency in Manchester, which was triggered following the resignation of the previous Labour MP Andrew Gwynne.
The election marks the first parliamentary by-election won by a Green Party candidate, and the first Green Party election win in the North of England.
Spencer will become the fifth current Green Party MP, with just under 41% of the vote, a lead of 12% on the second-place candidate, Matt Goodwin of Reform UK, who received just under 29% of the vote.
The election was highly anticipated as a test of confidence for the current Labour government, which has seen numerous high-profile scandals over past months.
The Labour candidate received 25% of the vote, dropping 25% from the 50% won at the 2024 general election.
The seat was previously regarded as the sixth safest seat for the party in Britain, and had not been lost by a Labour Party candidate since 1931.

Mayor of Greater Manchester Andy Burnham had applied to stand as the party's candidate, but was blocked by its National Executive Committee over a worry that Labour would lose the resulting by-election for Mayor, and amid fears he would mount a leadership challenge against Prime Minister Keir Starmer.

Former Deputy Leader of the Labour Party and former Deputy Prime Minister Angela Rayner said that "This result must be a wake up call" amid the election adding to mounting internal party pressure on Keir Starmer to resign following the election, which would trigger a leadership election within his party.
Starmer said in a statement that he was not planning to resign over the election results.
The Reform UK candidate Matt Goodwin's 29% of the vote was up 15% from the party's position in the constituency at the 2024 general election.

Talking to BBC News reporters, Goodwin blamed the Green Party win on "a coalition of Islamists and woke progressives that came together to dominate a constituency", and said "many people in this country will look at Gorton and Denton and be appalled by what they see."
The Conservative and Liberal Democrat parties both won just under 2% of the vote, with the Conservatives dropping 6% from the previous election, and the Liberal Democrats dropping 2%.

It is just the second time the Conservative Party has lost their deposit (which occurs by receiving under 5% of the vote) since 1962, and is the worst result in a by-election for the party in history.
The election and its campaign period has seen numerous allegations of misconduct.

The Reform campaign was alleged to have breached campaign laws by not imprinting statutory material clarifying the publisher on a public letter addressed from pensioner and Reform UK worker Patricia Clegg mailed to households in the constituency and printed to appear handwritten.
The Reform candidate Goodwin was acquitted by the High Court in a related case the day before the election.

The Green Party reported the Labour candidate Angeliki Stogia to police on election day after a campaign van not bearing the aforementioned imprint was pictured driving past polling stations, with text alleging the Greens wanted to "legalise all drugs and teach our children to use drugs" and "let our daughters be used for legal prostitution".
The Electoral Commission says on its website that campaigners must not drive or park vehicles "heavily branded with campaign material" near polling stations.

items.title: Caloundra wins first game in Australian soccer's Football Queensland Premier League 2 competition

s: Caloundra got their first season in the Football Queensland Premier League 2 (FQPL 2) competition underway with a 4 goals to 2 win over Brisbane Knights FC at their home ground in Meridan Plains, Australia on Saturday night.
"Starting the game that quickly, it just makes life a lot easier," Caloundra player Ethan Galbraith said.
"It was surprising but amazing at the same time.
I think we started fast like we wanted to.
And we got on top.
And once you do that to a team, obviously it makes it hard for them to get back into it.
But credit to them.
Second half with the man down, they really battled and made it difficult for us.
It's obviously a tough place to come.
Travel up the Coast on a weekend."
It was a tough away trip for the Brisbane Knights.
Their first twenty minutes were slow with a bit of ill-discipline, according to their coach, Rob Shaw.
"[It] cost us, I think, in that first half," Shaw said.
"[We] changed shape in the second half, showed, the boys settled, started to play football, a little bit better football.
It actually worked in some ways, even the man down.
The boys worked hard.
It was a bit of a mountain to climb, though, after the first half, but can't fault the effort though from the boys."
Caloundra will now travel to play Moreton City Excelsior while Brisbane Knights host the Samford Rangers.
"I think they're a pretty tough team," Galbraith said.
"We'll be up against it next week but looking forward to the challenge.
They've got a lot of good players in there. [They're a] very good team.
So we'll be up against it but ready for it."

items.title: Randwick City Council opens public consultation about parking near beaches: ''To pay or not to pay?''

s: On Wednesday, Randwick City Council, a municipality on the east coast of Sydney, New South Wales, Australia, opened a public consultation period focused on introducing parking fees at beaches within the Randwick area.
The consultation, affecting up to thousands of beachgoers in peak hours on hot summer weekends, is set to close on April 15.

The council mailed the consultation paper version to all residents and added to Randwick's "Have Your Say" portal with an online form and a note that feedback may also be provided by phone and in person.

The Council noted the beaches received a lot of non-local traffic, allegedly reaching 84% at certain beaches, according to mobile phone data collected by Veitch Lister Consulting (VLC), a United Kingdom and Australian firm.
The revenue from paid parking would help towards beaches cleaning, maintenance, and improving the quality of amenities, the Council wrote on the public consultation page.
The Council estimated implementing the proposal would require A$3.6 million expenditure and would generate yearly A$6 million revenue.
Randwick includes the Clovelly, Coogee, Maroubra, Malabar, Little Bay (Malabar Beach), La Perouse (Frenchmans Bay) and Yarra Bay areas.
The proposal stated that new signage and parking meters would be installed in late 2026 and 2027 if the proposal was approved.
A Wikinews contributor visited the area, noting previously the parking was time-limited but predominantly free, with selected sections designated as paid parking.
Parking at Arden St. was free, while parking at Coogee Oval or near Coogee Pavilion required a fee from 2003 to 2016.
Meanwhile, parking near Manly and Bondi beaches outside the Randwick area required a fee in many spots and streets immediately adjacent to the beach as of 2026.
Near Manly, a multi-level paid car park was available in a nearby shopping center.

items.title: US President Donald Trump appears to wear makeup after apparent rash breaks out on neck, reports say

s: On Tuesday, a rash that reporters had observed on US President Donald Trump's neck in photos from a Medal of Honor ceremony at the White House one day earlier appeared to have been covered up.
One media source indicated the substance used was cosmetic makeup, although Trump's physician, Dr. Sean Barbabella, told the source the rash had been covered up by a "very common cream."
President Trump has worn makeup in public before.
He once wore makeup to obscure bruises on his hands, which White House press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, stated were inflicted from "shaking hands all day every day.
Trump himself has attributed the bruises to his use of aspirin, of which he says he takes excessive amounts.
Trump said, "They say aspirin is good for thinning out the blood, and I don’t want thick blood pouring through my heart.
I want nice, thin blood pouring through my heart.
Does that make sense?"

items.title: Monta publishes its 2025 EV charger ranking, including hardware performance

s: The Danish firm Monta published a performance ranking of electric vehicle (EV) chargers on Wednesday.
The firm analysed 260,000 EV chargers connected to its platform, which were located in Europe.
In the publication, the firm showed the chargers ranked by their "performance score".
The firm calculated this score metric from two parameters — the charger uptime, and the percent of charge sessions that went successful without hardware or software or user interruptions.
The AC — slower chargers — and DC — fast chargers — ranking was provided in two separate tables.
AC chargers performance was topped by a Mennekes EV charger, with performance score 94.65.
Among DC chargers, five charger models by Alpitronic took the top spots, with performance score reaching 96.54.

The Driven, an Australian news site, noted that '9 out of 10' of the top performing DC chargers from Monta's report were available for sale, and were in use — by Ampol AmpCharge and BP Pulse — in Australia.
The firm noted the published results provided motivation for EV chargers to adopt these benchmarks in marketing, and further develop their products to increase performance and uptime.

A volunteer Wikinews reporter reached out to Monta, and Monta has clarified that they also have some EV chargers on their platform in Asia, Oceania, and North America, however excluded them from the ranking due to small quantities.
Monta also noted they were planning to release quarterly EV charger updates in 2026, and yearly EV charger ranking reports with awards.
The Monta's EV charger ranking program was launched in June last year.
Monta won the best EV app/software at the E-Mobility Awards 2023.

items.title: Moreton Bay illegally evicted homeless campers, Queensland Supreme Court rules

s: This past Friday, Justice Paul Smith of the Supreme Court of Queensland ruled that the City of Moreton Bay Council, immediately north of Brisbane, Australia, acted unlawfully when it removed several homeless people camping in public parks last year.

The court concluded the Council breached the law by providing insufficient time for the homeless people to find alternative accommodation and by disposing of their personal belongings without consent.

In the judgement, Justice Smith said the Council made "errors of law" finding that the Council's seizure and disposal of the property of eight homeless people at Eddie Hyland Park — including their tents and other personal belongings — without consent in April and May last year violated human rights.
Although the eviction involved eight campers at the park, the legal case was brought by eleven applicants who said they were affected by the Council's enforcement actions.
The judgement noted that the Council would still be allowed to remove campers from public parks provided this was done "lawfully".
On Friday, the Council published a statement noting that eight homeless people had taken the Council to court and linking to the Supreme Court judgement.
In that statement Council stated it would continue enforcing its ban on camping on public land.
Responsibility for providing shelter to homeless people rested with the Queensland state government according to the Council.
The court scheduled the next hearing in three weeks to determine relief and costs.
Basic Rights Queensland and the Queensland Human Rights Commission supported the campers in the legal proceedings.
The Council's actions followed its decision earlier in February last year to ban camping on public land, which made camping illegal on public land within the Council from March 12, 2025.

items.title: Australia grants refuge to five Iranian women's national soccer team players

s: Early Tuesday morning, Australia government officials issued humanitarian visas to five members of Iran's national women's football team.

The players refused to sing the Iranian anthem while at the Women's Asian Cup last week. if the visas had not been granted, the five players potentially faced serious punishment on their return to Iran, as Iranian media has labeled them "traitors".
Tony Burke, Minister for Home Affairs of Australia, sent a message on X on Tuesday stating that the five players were "welcome to stay in Australia, to be safe and have a home here".
The players are Zahra Ghanbari (captain), Fatemeh Pasandideh, Zahra Sarbali, Atefeh Ramezanizadeh, and Mona Hamoudi.
Tuesday afternoon, however, the rest of the Iranian national women's soccer team travelled to Gold Coast airport by bus.
As of Tuesday morning, authorities said these remaining Iranian women's soccer team members had not requested asylum, though were welcomed to do so.
Protesters surrounded the bus and some were lying on the ground to stop the bus, and had to be moved by police.

Due to reported threats from Iranian media and officials, in Australia, local police worked with the authorities and provided a safe place for the players to stay, as well as increased presence when the players were traveling.

items.title: Former Major League Baseball pitcher Julio Teherán retires

s: Julio Teherán, a two-time Major League Baseball All-Star, announced his retirement from baseball on Monday, at the age of 35.
The decision came two days after he was scratched from a scheduled start for Team Colombia in the 2026 World Baseball Classic (WBC) due to a shoulder injury.
Teherán had helped Team Colombia secure a 3-1 victory over Team Panama in the WBC before announcing his retirement.
Teherán had a thirteen-year MLB career, during which he primarily played for the Atlanta Braves, but also played for the Los Angeles Angels, Detroit Tigers, Milwaukee Brewers, and New York Mets.
He made his MLB debut with the Braves in 2011 at the age of 20 and spent his first nine seasons with the team, earning All-Star selections in 2014 and 2016.
Over his MLB career, Teherán compiled a 81-82 record, with a 3.85 ERA, 1.223 WHIP, and 1,260 strikeouts in 1,470.2 innings.
He had spent the 2022 and 2025 seasons playing in the Mexican Baseball League.

items.title: PM of Australia sends E-7A Wedgetail and air-to-air missiles to UAE

s: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said that, in response to United Arab Emirates call for help, Australia would deploy E-7A Wedgetail, a long-range reconnaissance plane, to help Gulf Arab states defend against attacks from Iran.
The Australian Defence Force said the plane is able to survey four million square kilometers with a powerful radar.
Government officials said the plane would be manned by around 85 Australian defence force (ADF) personnel.
Additionally, Australia would supply middle range air to air missiles, at the request of United Arab Emirates, that could down enemy's drones.
Foreign affairs correspondent at ABC News, Stephen Dziedzic, published a piece on Wednesday noting that from a legal perspective, Australia is at war.
He stated that not being an attacker, and not entering Iran, did not preclude Australia from joining a war.

The correspondent referenced article 51 from United Nations charter about "collective self-defence", which could involve, for example, providing support or intelligence to one of the participants of a war.
The correspondent raised concern that move could make Australia a potential target for attacks from, for example, Iran.

items.title: NSW government proposes rezoning to create residences midway between Sydney and Parramatta

s: The government of New South Wales (NSW), Australia announced plans to rezone the 113-hectare Burwood North precinct this Tuesday.
The plan included building 18,300 new homes in the area, and building a new metro station.
This would position the area as a residential hub between Sydney CBD and Parramatta, shortening commute times down to ten minutes, the proposal said.

With allowance for up to 42 storey residential buildings, the government proposal involved a requirement that at least 5% of the new homes were "affordable housing", offered at a lower rental price to lower income households.
Burwood North Station, scheduled to open in 2032, would provide easier access to retail outlets and businesses located near Parramatta Road, and reduce load on existing train and bus networks.
The proposal text noted it would create 3,900 new jobs to implement the changes.
The proposal was a part of Parramatta Road Corridor Urban Transformation Strategy.
The NSW Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure was listed as a contact for inquiries and feedback.

items.title: US president Donald Trump demands the unconditional surrender of Iran

s: Last Friday, United States President Donald Trump demanded the "unconditional surrender" of Iran via his Truth Social platform.
The declaration came as the war in Iran had gone on for a week.
Trump has also demanded more "acceptable" leadership in the country.
Trump wrote that once "acceptable" leadership was selected in Iran, the US and its allies would make Iran "economically bigger, better, and stronger than ever before."
On Saturday, in an address to the nation, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said that Trump's demand is a "dream they should send to their grave."
A week ago, the United States and Israel attacked Iran, and killed various government officials, including the supreme leader of Iran, Ali Khamenei, in strikes.
In retaliation for the attacks, Iran has bombed Middle Eastern countries including Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, and Oman, according to SBS News.
In the Saturday address, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian apologized for attacks on regional countries, Jakarta Globe reported.
The Globe also reported that 1,230 people were killed in Iran and that six US troops were killed.
Leavitt has stated that the war would likely last four to six weeks.

items.title: Australian Minister for Energy lowers fuel standards for 60 days amid rising oil prices, panic buying

s: Chris Bowen, Australian Minister for Climate Change and Energy, allowed the usage of dirtier fuel with elevated sulfur content for 60 days, he announced on Thursday.
As a part of the change, the oil refineries were required to prioritise supply to farmers in rural areas.
This decision followed issues with oil exports caused by the ongoing Middle East conflict, as fuel prices rose rapidly to over A$2/L.
The lower quality oil was previously exported to countries with lower fuel standards.
With the new temporarily changes in place, it would now be allowed to be used in Australia.
One of the two oil refineries, Ampol, noted rural areas supply would be prioritised.
Additionally, Bowen announced Australia would release 100 million liters from its reserve oil supply per month, in response to a request from the International Energy Agency (IEA).
The issue appeared related to the growing demand while supply was essentially unchanged.
As people stockpiled fuel, and the demand has doubled, there were concerns over panic buying by Australians.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese commented on longer term impacts of the situation on economics in Australia, talking with ABC Television on Thursday.

President of the National Farmer Federation commented noting the government regulation was direly needed in this situation as farmers and fishers were struggling to access fuel, especially in remote areas.

He also noted that government should prepare strategies in case the situation 'deteriorates', mentioning access to diesel was a pre-requisite for the farmers running the agricultural areas, collecting crops, transporting crops, and providing food to the country.
In reserve, Australia had 36 days worth of petrol, 32 days worth of diesel, and 29 days worth of jet fuel, respectively.
These fell short of the 90 days requirement under obligations for the IEA, of which Australia is a member.
Opposition was calling on the government to ensure fuel security, ABC News reported.
